arXiv:1907.04769v3 [quant-ph] 13 Apr 2020

Improving Variational Quantum Optimization using CVaR

Panagiotis Kl. Barkoutsos Affiliation: IBM Research – Zurich    Giacomo Nannicini Affiliation: IBM T.J. Watson Research Center    Anton Robert Affiliation: IBM Research – Zurich Affiliation: École Normale Supérieure, PSL University, Paris    Ivano Tavernelli Affiliation: IBM Research – Zurich    Stefan Woerner Email: wor@zurich.ibm.com Affiliation: IBM Research – Zurich
Abstract

Hybrid quantum/classical variational algorithms can be implemented on noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers and can be used to find solutions for combinatorial optimization problems. Approaches discussed in the literature minimize the expectation of the problem Hamiltonian for a parameterized trial quantum state. The expectation is estimated as the sample mean of a set of measurement outcomes, while the parameters of the trial state are optimized classically. This procedure is fully justified for quantum mechanical observables such as molecular energies. In the case of classical optimization problems, which yield diagonal Hamiltonians, we argue that aggregating the samples in a different way than the expected value is more natural. In this paper we propose the Conditional Value-at-Risk as an aggregation function. We empirically show – using classical simulation as well as quantum hardware – that this leads to faster convergence to better solutions for all combinatorial optimization problems tested in our study. We also provide analytical results to explain the observed difference in performance between different variational algorithms.

1 Introduction

Combinatorial optimization (CO) has been extensively studied, because it is applied in many areas of business and science, and it is a source of interesting mathematical problems [nemhauser1988]. Even if many CO problems are NP-hard, they are routinely solved (possibly not to provable optimality) in industrial applications. It is widely believed that quantum computers cannot solve such problems in polynomial time (i.e., NP ⊈\not\subseteq BQP [bernstein1997quantum]), but there is significant effort toward designing quantum algorithms that could be practically useful by quickly finding near-optimal solutions to these hard problems. Among these algorithms, two candidates are more likely to be efficiently implementable on noisy quantum computers: the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) [moll2018quantum, fried2017qtorch], and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [Farhi2014, farhi2017quantum, crooks2018performance]. Both VQE and QAOA use a parametrized quantum circuit U⁡(θ)U(\theta) (also called variational form) to generate trial wave functions |ψ⁡(θ)⟩=U⁡(θ)​|0⟩\ket{\psi(\theta)}=U(\theta)\ket{0}, guided by a classical optimization algorithm that aims to solve:

minθ⁡⟨ψ⁡(θ)|​H​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩.\displaystyle\min_{\theta}\bra{\psi(\theta)}H\ket{\psi(\theta)}. (1)

This expression encodes the total energy of a system through its Hamiltonian HH, and more specifically its expected value ⟨ψ⁡(θ)|​H​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩\bra{\psi(\theta)}H\ket{\psi(\theta)}. There is a well-known transformation to map CO problems into a Hamiltonian, see e.g., [lucas2014ising]; this will also be discussed subsequently in this paper. Empirical evaluations indicate that VQE’s performance suffers from some key weaknesses in the context of CO problems, and there is significant room for improvement [Nannicini2019]. At the same time, the literature on QAOA paints a mixed picture: while some work concludes that QAOA has promise [crooks2018performance, niu2019optimizing], other papers indicate that it may not perform better than classical algorithms [hastings2019classical].

In this paper, we propose a modification to the problem (1) that is given to the classical optimization algorithm: rather than minimizing the expected value ⟨ψ⁡(θ)|​H​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩\bra{\psi(\theta)}H\ket{\psi(\theta)}, we minimize its Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) – a measure that takes into account only the tail of the probability distribution and is widely used in finance [acerbi2002coherence]. We argue that CVaR more closely matches the practical goal of heuristic solution methods for CO problems. We provide an analytical and numerical study, showing that the proposed methodology significantly improves performance and robustness of VQE and QAOA in the context of CO. As a byproduct of this analysis, we find that for small-depth circuits it is important to use variational forms with a sufficient number of parameters, e.g., at least linear in the number of qubits. QAOA for fixed (small) depth does not satisfy this requirement, and produces “flat” quantum states that yield low probability of sampling the optimal solution. Thus, not only does our paper introduce a simple way to improve the performance of the two most prominent candidates for CO on noisy quantum computers, but it also sheds some light on their behavior with small-depth circuits. While we do not claim that this brings their performance on par with state-of-the-art classical heuristics, our results indicate a marked improvement as compared to what is proposed in the literature. The numerical experiments discussed in this paper are implemented in the open-source library Qiskit [Qiskit], and executed on classical quantum simulators as well as IBM’s quantum hardware.

The rest of this paper is divided as follows. The next two sections set the context for this paper by giving an overview of key concepts from the literature: the mapping of CO problems as a Hamiltonian, VQE (Section 2), and QAOA (Section 3). Section 4 formally introduces our main contribution, CVaR optimization. An analysis of the method is given in Section 5. Section provides an empirical evaluation of the proposed method on classically simulated quantum circuits, and using quantum hardware. Section provides a formal analysis of certain aspects of QAOA to explain the experimentally observed behavior. Finally, Section concludes the paper.

2 Variational Quantum Eigensolver

The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a hybrid quantum/classical algorithm originally proposed to approximate the ground state of a quantum chemical system, i.e., the state attaining the minimum energy [Peruzzo2014]. This is achieved by solving a problem of the form (1), with HH encoding the total energy of the quantum chemical system. The same approach can be used to attempt to solve CO problems. Consider a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem on nn variables:

minx∈{0,1}n⁡bT​x+xT​A​x,\displaystyle\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}b^{T}x+x^{T}Ax, (2)

for given b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. Using the variable transformation xi=(1−zi)/2x_{i}=(1-z_{i})/2 for zi∈{−1,+1}z_{i}\in\{-1,+1\}, problem (2) can be expressed as an Ising spin glass model:

minz∈{−1,+1}n⁡cT​z+zT​Q​z,\displaystyle\min_{z\in\{-1,+1\}^{n}}c^{T}z+z^{T}Qz, (3)

where cc and QQ are easily computed from (2). These two equivalent problems encompass binary optimization problems, i.e., CO problems, and they are NP-hard [barahona1982computational].

Problem (3) can be translated into a Hamiltonian for an nn-qubit system: we replace ziz_{i} by the Pauli Z-matrix

σZi\displaystyle\sigma_{Z}^{i} =\displaystyle= (100−1)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{array}\right)

acting on the ii-th qubit, and each term of the form zi​zjz_{i}z_{j} by σZi⊗σZj\sigma_{Z}^{i}\otimes\sigma_{Z}^{j}. The summation of (tensor products of) Pauli terms obtained this way is the desired Hamiltonian. The eigenvalues ±1\pm 1 of σZi\sigma_{Z}^{i} correspond to the positive and negative spin of (3). After constructing HH, we can apply VQE to attempt to determine the ground state, from which an optimal solution to (3) can be sampled with probability 1.

The choice of the variational form U⁡(θ)U(\theta) is important. In this paper we follow a standard approach, see e.g., [kandala2017hardware, Nannicini2019]. Assuming nn qubits, we start by applying single-qubit Y-rotations to every qubit, parametrized by an angle θ0,i\theta_{0,i} for qubit ii. We then repeat the following pp times: we apply controlled Z-gates to all qubit pairs (i,j)(i,j) satisfying i<ji<j, where ii denotes the control qubit and jj the target qubit; and we add another layer of single-qubit Y-rotations to every qubit, parametrized by θk,i\theta_{k,i} for qubit ii and repetition k∈{1,…,p}k\in\{1,\dots,p\}. Fig. 1 illustrates such a variational form for n=3n=3 and p=2p=2. Notice that this variational form span all basis states. Overall, this leads to n⁡(1+p)n(1+p) parametrized Y-rotations, and n⁡(n−1)2​p\frac{n(n-1)}{2}p controlled Z-gates. Since the controlled Z-gates commute with each other, the total circuit depth is O⁡(n​p)O(np), although the number of gates is quadratic in nn. This variational form is used in our numerical simulations. When experimenting on quantum hardware we use nearest neighbor controlled Z-gates rather than all-to-all, i.e., we follow the connectivity provided by the hardware to reduce the number of two-qubit gates. We remark that these variational forms span any basis state (and thus the ground state of a diagonal Hamiltonian) already with the first layer of Y-rotations. The purpose of subsequent layers is to hopefully facilitate the task for the classical optimization algorithm used to choose the variational parameters. The above variational form with just one layer of Y-rotations can be efficiently simulated classically; for a discussion on the effect of entangling gates, we refer to [Nannicini2019].

The classical optimization algorithm that attempts to solve (1) must be able to (at least) compute the objective function, i.e., the expected value in (1). This is difficult to compute directly, but it can be estimated as follows. First, we prepare the trial wavefunction |ψ⁡(θ)⟩\ket{\psi(\theta)} on a quantum processor. Then, we measure the qubits, resulting in an nn-bit string x0​…​xn−1x_{0}\dots x_{n-1}. Each observed string easily translates into a sample from ⟨ψ⁡(θ)|​H​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩\bra{\psi(\theta)}H\ket{\psi(\theta)}, because HH is a weighted summation of tensor products of Pauli Z-matrices, and each such term can be computed with a simple parity check. We denote these samples by Hk​(θ)H_{k}(\theta), k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, where K∈ℕK\in\mathbb{N} is the number of samples. The sample mean

1K​∑k=1KHk​(θ)\displaystyle\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}H_{k}(\theta) (7)

is an estimator for ⟨ψ⁡(θ)|​H​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩\bra{\psi(\theta)}H\ket{\psi(\theta)}, and is used as the objective function for the classical optimization algorithm. The solution returned by the algorithm is then given by the bitstring that leads to the smallest HkH_{k} among all observed bitstrings and all θ\theta that have been evaluated.

3 Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a hybrid quantum/classical algorithm specifically developed for CO problems. In the context of this paper, QAOA can be seen as a form of VQE with a specific choice of the variational form that is derived from the problem Hamiltonian HH [Farhi2014]. QAOA enjoys stronger convergence properties than VQE. For some problems, it can be shown that QAOA determines a quantum state with a guaranteed approximation ratio with respect to the ground state [Farhi2014, farhi2014e3lin2]; furthermore, QAOA applies adiabatic evolution as the circuit depth goes to ∞\infty, implying that it will determine the optimal solution of the CO problem if the depth of the variational form is large enough and we can find the optimal circuit parameters.

Given a problem Hamiltonian corresponding to a QUBO as defined in (3), the variational form of QAOA is constructed with a layer of Hadamard gates, followed by two alternating unitaries:

UC​(γ)\displaystyle U_{C}(\gamma) =\displaystyle= e−i​γ​(∑i=1nci​σZi+∑i,j=1nQi​j​σZi⊗σZj),\displaystyle e^{-i\gamma\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\sigma_{Z}^{i}+\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\sigma_{Z}^{i}\otimes\sigma_{Z}^{j}\right)}, (8)
UB​(β)\displaystyle U_{B}(\beta) =\displaystyle= e−iβ∑i=1nσXi,\displaystyle e^{-i\beta\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{X}^{i}}, (9)

where σXi\sigma_{X}^{i} denotes the Pauli X-matrix

σXi\displaystyle\sigma_{X}^{i} =\displaystyle= (0110)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ 1&0\end{array}\right)

acting on the ii-th qubit. For a given depth p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, the variational form is thus defined as:

U⁡(β,γ)\displaystyle U(\beta,\gamma) =\displaystyle= [∏i=1pUB​(βi)​UC​(γi)]​H⊗n,\displaystyle\left[\prod_{i=1}^{p}U_{B}(\beta_{i})U_{C}(\gamma_{i})\right]H^{\otimes n}, (13)

where β,γ∈ℝp\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{p} are vectors of variational parameters, and here, HH denotes a Hadamard gate. (The symbol HH is overloaded in the quantum computing literature; in this paper it generally denotes the Hamiltonian, and in the few occasions where it indicates a Hadamard gate, we note it explicitly.) This yields the trial wave function:

|ψ⁡(β,γ)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi(\beta,\gamma)} =\displaystyle= U⁡(β,γ)​|0⟩,\displaystyle U(\beta,\gamma)\ket{0}, (14)

which replaces |ψ⁡(θ)⟩\ket{\psi(\theta)} in (1). As in VQE, the expected value is computed as the sample mean over multiple observations from the quantum state, and the algorithm returns the bitstring that leads to the smallest HkH_{k} among all observed bitstrings and choices of β,γ\beta,\gamma.

The number of variational parameters for QAOA is thus 2​p2p, compared to n⁡(1+p)n(1+p) for VQE. The circuit depth of the QAOA variational form depends on nn, pp, and the number of clauses in the problem Hamiltonian, which is a difference with respect to VQE. Every UBU_{B} requires nn single-qubit X-rotations. One way to construct UCU_{C} requires a single-qubit Z-rotation for each ci≠0c_{i}\neq 0, and a single-qubit Z-rotation plus two CNOT-gates for each Qi​j≠0Q_{ij}\neq 0, yielding the term e−iγσZi⊗σZje^{-i\gamma\sigma_{Z}^{i}\otimes\sigma_{Z}^{j}} up to a global phase. The circuits used in our implementation are described in Appendix . In total, this leads to O⁡(n2​p)O(n^{2}p) single-qubit rotations and O⁡(n2​p)O(n^{2}p) CNOT-gates, but the scaling may be better than the worst case if QQ is sparse (i.e., there are few two-qubit interactions).

4 CVaR Optimization

In quantum mechanics observables are defined as expected values ⟨ψ|​H​|ψ⟩\bra{\psi}H\ket{\psi}. This leads to the natural choice of the sample mean (7) as the objective function for the classical optimization problems embedded in VQE and QAOA. We argue that for problems with a diagonal Hamiltonian, such as CO problems, the sample mean may be a poor choice in practice. This is because when HH is diagonal, there exists a ground state which is a basis state. If determining the value Hj,jH_{j,j} of a basis state |j⟩\ket{j} is classically easy, the state with the minimum eigenvalue computed by an algorithm is simply the best measurement outcome among all measurements performed. It is therefore reasonable to focus on improving the properties of the best measurement outcome, rather than the average. We illustrate this intuition with a simple example. Consider two algorithms 𝒜1{\cal A}_{1} and 𝒜2{\cal A}_{2} applied to a problem with Hamiltonian HH, minimum eigenvalue λmin\lambda_{\min} and ground state |j⟩\ket{j}. Suppose 𝒜1{\cal A}_{1} produces a state |ψ1⟩\ket{\psi_{1}} and 𝒜2{\cal A}_{2} produces a state |ψ2⟩\ket{\psi_{2}}, with the following properties: ⟨ψ1|​H​|ψ1⟩/λmin=1.1\bra{\psi_{1}}H\ket{\psi_{1}}/\lambda_{\min}=1.1 and ⟨j|ψ1⟩=0\braket{j|\psi_{1}}=0; ⟨ψ2|​H​|ψ2⟩/λmin=2.0\bra{\psi_{2}}H\ket{\psi_{2}}/\lambda_{\min}=2.0 and ⟨j|ψ2⟩=0.1\braket{j|\psi_{2}}=0.1. We argue that from a practical point of view, algorithm 𝒜2{\cal A}_{2} is likely to be more useful than 𝒜1{\cal A}_{1}. This is because even if 𝒜1{\cal A}_{1} leads to samples with a better objective function value on average, 𝒜1{\cal A}_{1} will never yield the ground state |j⟩\ket{j}; whereas 𝒜2{\cal A}_{2}, which is much worse on average, has a positive and sufficiently high probability of yielding the ground state, so that with enough repetitions we can be almost certain of determining |j⟩\ket{j}.

In light of this discussion, one way to attain our goal would be to choose, as the objective function, the minimum observed outcome over a set of measurements: min⁡{H1,…,HK}\min\{H_{1},...,H_{K}\}. However, for finite KK this typically leads to a non-smooth, ill-behaved objective function that is difficult to handle for classical optimization algorithms.

To help smooth the objective function, while still focusing on improving the best measured outcomes rather than the average, we propose the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR, also called Expected Shortfall) as the objective function. Formally, the CVaR of a random variable XX for a confidence level α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1] is defined as

CVaRα​(X)\displaystyle\text{CVaR}_{\alpha}(X) =\displaystyle= 𝔼⁡[X|X≤FX−1​(α)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[X|X\leq F_{X}^{-1}(\alpha)] (15)

where FXF_{X} denotes the cumulative density function of XX. In other words, CVaR is the expected value of the lower α\alpha-tail of the distribution of XX. Without loss of generality, assume that the samples HkH_{k} are sorted in nondecreasing order, i.e. Hk+1≥HkH_{k+1}\geq H_{k}. Then, for a given set of samples {Hk}k=1,…,K\{H_{k}\}_{k=1,\dots,K} and value of α\alpha, the CVaRα\text{CVaR}_{\alpha} is defined as

1⌈α​K⌉​∑k=0⌈α​K⌉Hk.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\lceil\alpha K\rceil}\sum_{k=0}^{\lceil\alpha K\rceil}H_{k}. (16)

Note that the limit α↘0\alpha\searrow 0 corresponds to the minimum, and α=1\alpha=1 corresponds to the expected value of XX. In this sense, CVaR is a generalization of both the sample mean (7), and the best observed sample min⁡{H1,…,HK}\min\{H_{1},...,H_{K}\}. For small, nonzero values of α\alpha, CVaR still puts emphasis on the best observed samples, but it leads to a smoother and easier to handle objective function. It is clear that this can be applied to both VQE and QAOA, simply by replacing the sample mean (7) with CVaRα\text{CVaR}_{\alpha} in the classical optimization algorithm. We call the resulting algorithms CVaR-VQE and CVaR-QAOA, respectively.

5 Analysis of CVaR Optimization

The optimization of CVaRα\text{CVaR}_{\alpha} with α<1\alpha<1 modifies the landscape of the objective function of VQE and QAOA as compared to the expected value, i.e., α=1\alpha=1. This is formalized next.

We need to define a random variable that encodes the classical objective function value of a measurement outcome, i.e., the value of a binary string in the QUBO problem. Let X⁡(θ)X(\theta) be the random variable with outcomes Hj,jH_{j,j} for j∈{0,1}nj\in\{0,1\}^{n}, i.e., the diagonal elements of the Hamiltonian, and Prob​(X⁡(θ)=Hj,j)=|αj​(θ)|2\text{Prob}(X(\theta)=H_{j,j})=|\alpha_{j}(\theta)|^{2} where |ψ⁡(θ)⟩=∑jαj​(θ)​|j⟩\ket{\psi(\theta)}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}(\theta)\ket{j}. In other words, X⁡(θ)X(\theta) represents the QUBO objective function associated with a single measurement taken on the quantum state |ψ⁡(θ)⟩\ket{\psi(\theta)}. Then the CVaR-version of (1) can be written as:

minθ⁡CVaRα​(X⁡(θ)).\displaystyle\min_{\theta}\text{CVaR}_{\alpha}(X(\theta)). (17)

As it turns out, there is no well-defined mapping between local minima of (1) and (17).

Proposition 5.1

A local minimum of (1) does not necessarily correspond to a local minimum of (17), and vice versa.

To show this, we first exhibit a local minimum of (1) that is not a local minimum of (17). Consider a two-qubit Hamiltonian H=diag​(0,1,1,2)H=\text{diag}(0,1,1,2), and variational form depicted in Fig. .
